claim: Of the 103 passages in the pur- corpus at the stanza unit, 21 state a count of the fort word and 82 state none.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, 49 numeral rows over 30 passages, 29 adjudicated COUNTS-PUR over 21 distinct stanzas; built by 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-counts.py and rv-pur-counts-adjudicate.py
notes: Denominator 103 = the etymological pur- family at the stanza unit (106 tokens, 104 padas, 103 stanzas, 86 hymns). 82 of 103 is 79.6 percent of the corpus carrying NO count. Any statement of the form 'the Rigveda says there were N forts' is drawn from a fifth of the passages that mention forts at all.

claim: Among the 21 passages stating a count of forts, 100 is stated in 8, ninety-nine in 6, seven in 4, ninety in 2, and 'hundreds' (satani, plural) in 1; two of the ninety-nine passages add an ordinal 'the hundredth'.
notes: Counts sum to 21 distinct passages; the two 'hundredth' passages are inside the 99 set and are not counted twice. The constitution's four enumerated headings (90, 99, 100, other counts) are all attested, and 'other counts' resolves to seven and to the unbounded plural 'hundreds'.

claim: Ninety-nine is NOT the modal count of forts in the Rigveda. One hundred is, by 8 passages to 6.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv as PUR4J-002. 8 passages state 100 and 6 state 99; counting the plural 'hundreds' of RV 6.31.4 with the hundreds makes it 9 to 6.
notes: This answers directly the question the reconciliation brief left open at section 2.6 item 2 ('whether 99 is the modal count, the maximal count, or merely the most quotable'). It is neither modal nor maximal: 100, 'hundreds' and 1000 are all larger, and 100 is more frequent. It is the most quotable. The figure that titles the inherited RV-01 specification and the the-forts page headline is the second most common count in the corpus.

claim: Ninety-nine is never expressed by a single numeral. In all six passages it is two words, nava 'nine' and navati- 'ninety', joined by ca in three of them and separated by other words in four.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, expression column. RV 1.54.6d puro navatim dambhayo nava; 2.19.6c navatim ca nava; 4.26.3b nava sakam navatih; 7.19.5b nava yat puro navatim ca; 7.99.5b nava puro navatim ca; 8.93.2a nava yo navatim puro
notes: The reconciliation brief section 2.6 item 1 flagged that 'even 99 is attested is a claim about a reading'. Tested here and upheld: the reading is secure, because all three full-coverage translators independent of one another on this point (Griffith, Geldner, Grassmann) render 99 at all six, and the padapatha analyses the words separately. But the object is a two-word expression, not a numeral.

claim: navati- 'ninety' is a feminine SINGULAR collective governing a plural puras in five of the six ninety-nine passages; only at RV 4.26.3 does it appear as an agreeing plural navatih.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, numeral_morph column: case=ACC|gender=F|number=SG at RV 1.54.6, 2.19.6, 7.19.5, 7.99.5, 8.93.2 and at the two ninety passages 1.130.7 and 3.12.6; case=ACC|gender=F|number=PL at RV 4.26.3
notes: Consequence for method, not only for grammar: a numeral-noun AGREEMENT test scored on case, gender and number under-reports navati- by construction, returning PARTIAL for a numeral that governs its noun perfectly well. Six rows of the counts register record this override explicitly. A mechanical agreement test run without this correction would drop five of the six ninety-nine passages.

claim: The identical nava-plus-navati- expression counts RIVERS, not forts, at RV 10.104.8, in a stanza that also carries the fort-word epithet purbhid.
locator: RV 10.104.8c navatim srotya nava ca sravantir; padapatha navatim | srotyah | nava | ca | sravantih. Griffith 'nine-and-ninety flowing streams'; Geldner 'die neunundneunzig fliessenden Stroeme'; Grassmann 'Die neunundneunzig Fluesse'. purbhit in pada b is NOM.SG.M, an epithet of Indra, and takes no numeral.
notes: The control case for the whole counts unit. It is also the case that defeats a stanza-level co-occurrence measure: navati- and a pur- family lemma share this stanza, and the ninety-nine here has nothing to do with forts. 04-AUDITS/rigveda-pur-family-method.md section 7 measured navati- at 33.5x its corpus rate inside family stanzas and declined to read it; this row is why that restraint was correct.

claim: Sambara's forts are counted at ninety, ninety-nine, one hundred, 'the hundredth' and 'hundreds' across six passages. Every count value the constitution section 4J enumerates attaches to this one opponent.
locator: RV 1.130.7 ninety (sambaram in pada d); 2.14.6 one hundred (satam sambarasya puro); 2.19.6 ninety-nine (sambarasya); 4.26.3 ninety-nine plus the hundredth (sambarasya); 6.31.4 'hundreds' (satani sambarasya puro); 7.99.5 ninety-nine (sambarasya)
notes: A measurement, and the sharpest single piece of evidence in this unit. The count is not a stable property of the opponent it is most often attached to. Recorded as a count of passages, not as an interpretation of why they differ; what it implies is PUR4J-012.

claim: In two of the six ninety-nine passages the ninety-nine is immediately followed by an ordinal 'the hundredth', applied to a dwelling word rather than to the fort word.
locator: RV 4.26.3: pada a-b nava sakam navatih ... purah, pada c satatamam vesyam 'the hundredth dwelling/inhabitant'. RV 7.19.5: pada b nava yat puro navatim ca, pada c nivesane satatama 'the hundredth in the settlement'.
notes: The ninety-nine and the hundredth are one schema: ninety-nine plus one completes a hundred. Note that satatama- does not modify pur- in either passage, so a search for numerals attached to the fort word alone would miss the completion that gives the ninety-nine its shape.

claim: Every count of forts in the corpus is one of seven, ninety, ninety-nine, one hundred or 'hundreds'. No passage states an irregular figure.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, count_of_forts over all 29 COUNTS-PUR rows. The numeral inventory of the 103 passages was fixed independently by scanning the Grassmann gloss of all 721 distinct lemmas occurring in them for a German number word, returning 12 candidates, all adjudicated.
notes: Stated with its denominator: this is a property of the 21 counting passages, and the numeral inventory it is drawn from was built by an exhaustive scan of the corpus's own lexicon, not by looking for the numbers already expected. Two gloss-scan candidates were excluded with reasons recorded in 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-counts.py: satakratu- (an Indra epithet) and arya- (a false positive matching 'drei' inside Grassmann's gloss 'Angehoeriger der drei oberen Grosskasten').

claim: The 'seven forts' passages cluster with Purukutsa and the Puru, and the ninety-nine and one hundred passages with Divodasa, Atithigva and Sambara. The count co-varies with the narrative cycle, not with the opponent alone.
locator: Seven: RV 1.63.7 (purukutsa-, puru-, sudas-), 1.174.2 (purukutsa-), 6.20.10 (purukutsa-, puru-), 7.18.13 (puru-) — Purukutsa or Puru in all four. Ninety-nine and one hundred: divodasa- at RV 1.53.8, 1.130.7, 2.19.6, 4.26.3, 4.30.20, 6.31.4; sambara- at RV 1.130.7, 2.14.6, 2.19.6, 4.26.3, 6.31.4, 7.99.5.
notes: Cuts against a reading in which the numbers are freely interchangeable ornament: they are distributed by story, and 'seven autumnal forts' is close to verbatim at RV 1.174.2b and 6.20.10c. Lemma co-presence in a stanza, not a claim that any named figure is patron or opponent of that passage; the roles are established per passage in the fields register, not here.

claim: Among the counting passages, the seven-fort set is the most Archaic on Arnold's periodisation (3 of 4 Archaic) and the ninety-nine set is predominantly Strophic (4 of 6).
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-passages.csv joined to rigveda-pur-counts.csv. Seven: RV 1.63.7 A, 1.174.2 A, 6.20.10 A, 7.18.13 C. Ninety-nine: RV 1.54.6 C, 2.19.6 A, 4.26.3 S, 7.19.5 S, 7.99.5 S, 8.93.2 S.
notes: Small n, and carrying every caveat that already caps the stratum column: it rests on Arnold 1905 alone (DEP-001), the by-book second instrument returns a null (DEP-004), and PUR-028 holds at HYPOTHESIS that Arnold's periods are chronological stages at all. With n=4 and n=6 this is a description of ten passages and NOT a chronology of the fort count. It is recorded so that a later unit cannot present it as new.
